title: Education Gadfly Weekly, Volume 26, Number 43
author: Fordham Institute
summary: This issue of Fordham's Education Gadfly Weekly (Volume 26, Number 43) leads with Michael Petrilli's argument that states should act boldly on curriculum and instruction, following Mississippi's example. It pairs that with Meredith Coffey and David Griffith on what other states can learn from Alabama's literacy gains, and Chad Aldeman's rebuttal of the claim that American schools are resegregating. The reviews section covers a Jeff Murray analysis of NWEA MAP data showing positive signs of post-Covid recovery and an Alicia Anderson item on measuring future teacher potential when graduate hiring is soft. The new research item highlights Liana Loewus's report on how Alabama beat the odds in reading. The issue also promotes the Gadfly Show episode on Alabama, a research note that AI tutoring in college courses may hurt performance and engagement, and a Wonkathon call on rules for digital technology in schools.
points: The lead commentary urges states to use direct levers on curriculum and instruction rather than relying on indirect incentives.
Alabama's literacy gains are framed as the product of decades of sustained commitment rather than one reform.
Aldeman argues that integration has advanced greatly since the 1960s and that students need strong teaching and coursework regardless of classroom demographics.
Post-Covid test data show real recovery signs but vary by subject, grade and student group.
A cited study finds AI tutoring in college courses may reduce academic performance and engagement.
quotes: You can just do things" is one of those memes floating around the internet, and it fits well with the current enthusiasm for muscular state action around curriculum and instruction.
Alabama's gains are not the product of any single reform. They reflect decades of work and a sustained commitment to getting reading instruction right, from the statehouse to the classroom.

America has made enormous progress on integration since the 1960s, and there are good reasons to keep working toward it. But children can't wait for their schools to become more integrated before they get a good education.
They need challenging coursework, capable teachers, and adults who notice when they're falling behind—regardless of who their classmates happen to be.
The labor market for new college graduates appears unsteady, but that may be good news for schools: More young adults consider teaching when hiring in other fields slows down.
The newest test data from NWEA MAP show several unmistakably positive signs of academic recovery from post-Covid lows.

Our latest report reveals a state that has built an unusually comprehensive system for teaching children to read—anchored in the science of reading and driven by an informed, top-down policy structure; leaders who have stayed the course; and a robust coaching infrastructure.
